extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, constitutional historians, and educated general readers interested in forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative-political-theory checklist of qualities and defects used to evaluate constitutional forms (Electoral College vs Parliament/Cabinet vs Monarchy). Emphasizes representativeness, continuity, flexibility in crisis, incentives for statesmanship, intelligibility to the public, and the symbolic/social functions of monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electoral College discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: Deputies/electors ought to 'exercise a real discretion' and by independent choice select the President; they should not merely be 'messengers--a transmitter' who 'take a ticket, and drop that ticket in an urn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues the American Electoral College was intended to permit independent judgment by electors but in practice primary electors preselect and instruct deputies, turning the College into a farce. The anti-pattern is electors who mechanically follow instructions rather than choosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of the electoral body
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real electoral body' should be continuous in function rather than separating after electing its ruler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliament is praised because it 'does not, like the Electoral College in the United States, separate when it has elected its ruler; it watches, legislates, seats and unseats ministries, from day to day.' Continuity provides ongoing oversight and accountability; a one-off selecting body cannot perform these ongoing roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative composition of a choosing body
rubrics_metrics.description: The selecting body ought to 'represent the general average intelligence' of the country and 'represent the various special interests, special opinions, special prejudices'—having advocates for particular sects and a neutral, judicial-like body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good Parliament should be diverse and reflective of society's various interests so that it is the 'best selector of executives'—contrast with a national electorate which is less discerning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nation-as-constituency is vulnerable
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation itself, as a large constituency, is 'in all but the rarest cases, a bad constituency'—it is unskilled and easily manipulated by electioneering managers ('wire-pullers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large electorates require organization to avoid 'voting away' effectively; when voters act as parts of organizations they 'abdicate' their electoral function. The anti-pattern is relying on an unorganized mass electorate for discerning choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of executive and legislature (founders' intent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding the President's Ministers from the legislature preserves 'the legislative branch absolutely distinct from the executive branch' and prevents ministers from eclipsing the President.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation was seen as essential by the U.S. founders to prevent the legislature becoming the executive. The page acknowledges it as wise for the specific end of preserving separation, even while noting trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs of exclusion: incentive structure for public life
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding ministers from legislative office causes 'the degradation of public life' because unless legislators have prospect of action and responsibility, 'a first-rate man will not care to take the place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cabinet (fusion) system incentivizes continuous careers, responsibility, and active statesmanship; the anti-pattern is a legislature treated like a debating society detached from executive responsibility, which discourages top talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elasticity and reserve power in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution should have an 'ELASTIC element' or a 'REVOLUTIONARY RESERVE'—the ability to choose a ruler or change leadership suited to sudden emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabinet systems permit the selection or replacement of leaders in response to crises; Presidential systems with fixed terms are rigid ('no ELASTIC element') and cannot quickly adjust leadership when exigencies demand different qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding government by an 'unknown quantity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection mechanisms should avoid resulting in 'government by an UNKNOWN QUANTITY'—electing leaders about whom society has 'no living idea' or who are not public household names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cabinet governments tend to produce leaders who are known and whose characters are 'household IDEAS.' Presidential elections can lead to winners who are effectively unknown and thus risky in crisis; this is presented as a severe defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for leaders with crisis-appropriate qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Different qualities are needed in calm times and in crises; a system should allow bringing forward leaders with 'imperious will, rapid energy' for crises, even if they were not suitable for ordinary times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page uses historical examples to argue that constitutional forms should enable bringing in leaders fit for extraordinary occasions (e.g., Cavour, a 'statesman above all men') by lawful, flexible means rather than being stuck with inappropriate incumbents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligibility to the mass of mankind
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful government form is one that 'the mass of mankind understand'—monarchy is described as an 'intelligible government' compared to complex constitutional systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comprehension matters: when asked 'Will you be governed by a king, or will you be governed by a constitution?' many choose the simpler, imaginable option. Comprehensibility and psychological accessibility are treated as practical merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic and emotional functions (pageantry, family)
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal pageantry and a 'FAMILY on the throne' create accessible emotional events (marriages, ceremonies) that 'sweeten politics' and speak to 'men's bosoms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that such symbolic, seemingly 'irrelevant' facts engage large swathes of the population and foster attachment; anti-pattern is a purely technocratic polity that lacks such emotional touchstones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/sanctifying strength of monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Monarchy 'strengthens our Government with the strength of religion'; many subjects feel a 'mystic obligation to obey' the monarch rather than laws alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This quasi-religious veneration can cement the constitution by enlisting widespread credulous obedience. The page notes historical fluctuations in this sentiment and its political implications (both beneficial and harmful).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-partisan unifying role of the crown
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown 'is of no party' and its apparent separation from business 'removes it both from enmities and from desecration,' making it a visible symbol of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monarchy's aloofness and latent functions preserve its mystery and enable it to combine affection across conflicting parties; this non-partisan role is valuable in maintaining social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy as social head preventing politicized scramble
rubrics_metrics.description: A monarch as the visible head of society restrains low social ambition from becoming political competition; if the highest social rank were regularly contested in Parliament, 'social adventurers' would flock to politics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues that keeping a social head outside electoral competition reduces vulgar social ambition in politics and limits the transformation of Parliament into a mere scramble for conspicuous life.
